scene1: This video has no timeline and no editor.
It is code, written with Claude, and it renders the same way every time.
Let me show you how it works.
scene2: Remotion treats a video as a function of the frame number.
At thirty frames per second, frame forty-five is one and a half seconds.
There are no timers and no hidden state.
The same frame always produces the same picture.
scene3: Take one move, and give it three curves.
A linear move has a constant speed, and it feels flat.
An easing changes the feel without changing the distance.
Two numbers decide it: damping for the bounce, and stiffness for the speed.
scene4: Now the part that surprised us most: the voice comes first.
A voice has no timestamps, so we record it, measure it, and let the video follow.
A transcript gives every word a start and an end, and each sentence snaps to the pause before it.
The result is a small file that tells every scene exactly when to act.
scene5: That is how these captions work.
Each word pops in the moment it is spoken, and the word being spoken lights up.
Change the spring settings, and the whole feel changes with it.
scene6: Scenes can overlap, with a transition between each pair.
There is a voice, there are effects, and there is music that ducks under the voice, so you can always hear it.
All of it is placed by frame number, like everything else.
scene7: The camera is just math too.
A zoom is a scale, a pan is a translation, and a tilt is a rotation with perspective.
Here the view leans over by twenty degrees, then rolls back.
For real depth, Remotion can render three-dimensional scenes, with lights and an orbiting camera.
Add motion blur, and fast moves look as if a real lens filmed them.
scene8: Claude writes the scenes, the helpers, and the scripts.
You write the script, choose the voice, and judge the feel.
That is the whole idea: video as code.
